meta.titre: Refraction and lenses: refractive index, critical angle and the lens formula

sections.contenu_markdown: A fisherman at Kribi spears a fish that seems to be in one place, but misses because the fish is really deeper. A pair of reading glasses sold at a roadside stall in Ngaoundere makes small print clear thanks to a lens that bends light. Both effects come from refraction, the bending of light as it passes from one material into another. The GCE O/L paper asks you to use the refractive index, apparent depth, the critical angle and the lens formula, so it is a good topic for collecting marks.

items: Light travels in a straight line in a uniform medium, and the normal is drawn at right angles to the boundary.
The speed of light in air (and in a vacuum) is about $3.0 \times 10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
The sine of an angle can be found with a calculator, for example $\sin 30^\circ = 0.5$.

sections.titre: Refraction, refractive index and lens calculations
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Refraction** is the change in direction of a ray of light when it passes from one transparent medium into another, because its speed changes. Angles are measured between the ray and the **normal**.

- Passing into a denser medium (air to glass), the ray bends **towards** the normal; into a less dense medium it bends **away** from it.
- The **refractive index** of a medium, going from air into it:

$$n = \frac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \frac{\text{speed of light in air}}{\text{speed of light in the medium}}$$

where $i$ is the angle of incidence in air and $r$ the angle of refraction in the medium. A graph of $\sin i$ against $\sin r$ is a straight line through the origin whose gradient is $n$. The index has no unit.

- **Real and apparent depth.** An object under a transparent material seems nearer the surface when viewed from above:

$$n = \frac{\text{real depth}}{\text{apparent depth}}$$

**Lenses.** A convex lens converges light and a concave lens diverges it. The lens formula and magnification, in the **real-is-positive convention**, are:

$$\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{u} + \frac{1}{v} \qquad m = \frac{v}{u} = \frac{\text{image height}}{\text{object height}}$$

In this convention $u$ is positive for a real object; $v$ is positive for a real image and negative for a virtual image; $f$ is positive for a convex lens and negative for a concave lens. Always state this convention in your working before you use the formula.

variantes.nom: Total internal reflection and the critical angle
variantes.quand_utiliser: When light moves from a denser to a less dense medium (glass to air, water to air), or when optical fibres and prisms are involved.
variantes.contenu_markdown: When light travels from a denser to a less dense medium, the refracted ray bends away from the normal. At the **critical angle** $c$ the refracted ray runs along the boundary (angle $90^\circ$). If the angle of incidence is greater than $c$, all the light is reflected (**total internal reflection**). The conditions are: the light is in the denser medium, and $i > c$. The critical angle satisfies $\sin c = \dfrac{1}{n}$. Applications include optical fibres, prism reflectors in binoculars and "cat's-eye" reflectors.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When an object distance and focal length are given and you must find the image distance or size.
variantes.contenu_markdown: State the convention: real object distance $u > 0$, real image $v > 0$, virtual image $v < 0$, convex lens $f > 0$, concave lens $f < 0$. Rearrange $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u}$, calculate $v$, then $m = \dfrac{v}{u}$ and image height $= m \times$ object height. A negative $v$ means a virtual image on the same side as the object.

sections.enonce_markdown: A ray of light in air strikes a flat glass surface at an angle of incidence of $40^\circ$. The refractive index of the glass is $1.5$ and the speed of light in air is $3.0 \times 10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. (a) Calculate the angle of refraction. (b) Calculate the speed of light in the glass. (c) Calculate the critical angle of the glass and say what happens to a ray inside the glass meeting a glass-air boundary at $45^\circ$.

etapes.justification: From air into glass, $n = \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}$, so $\sin r = \dfrac{\sin i}{n}$.
Use the inverse sine on the calculator.
Since $n = \dfrac{\text{speed in air}}{\text{speed in glass}}$, the speed in glass is $\dfrac{\text{speed in air}}{n}$.
Total internal reflection occurs inside the denser medium when $i > c$.
etapes.resultat_markdown: $45^\circ > 41.8^\circ$, so the ray is totally internally reflected.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The angle of refraction is **25.4 degrees**, the speed in glass is **2.0 x 10^8 m/s**, the critical angle is **41.8 degrees**, and the ray meeting the boundary at 45 degrees undergoes **total internal reflection**.

items.erreur_markdown: A student writes $n = \dfrac{\sin r}{\sin i}$ for light going from air into glass and obtains $n < 1$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The refractive index of a material is greater than 1 for light going from air into it. The ratio has been inverted.
items.correction_markdown: Use $n = \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}$ with $i$ the angle in air.

items.erreur_markdown: A student measures the angle of incidence between the ray and the glass surface and finds $n$ with it.
items.pourquoi_faux: Angles in the law of refraction are measured from the normal, not from the boundary.
items.correction_markdown: Draw the normal and measure both angles from it.

items.erreur_markdown: A student calculates apparent depth as real depth multiplied by the refractive index, giving $9.0 \times 1.5 = 13.5\ \mathrm{cm}$.
items.pourquoi_faux: An object looks nearer the surface than it really is, so the apparent depth is smaller. The relation is $n = \text{real}/\text{apparent}$.

items.erreur_markdown: A student explains that total internal reflection happens when light goes from air into glass at a large angle.
items.pourquoi_faux: Total internal reflection occurs only when light moves from a denser to a less dense medium, and the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle.
items.correction_markdown: Say that light must be in the denser medium (glass or water) and $i > c$.

items.erreur_markdown: A student uses $\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{u} + \dfrac{1}{v}$ with a positive $f$ for a concave lens and gets a real image.
items.pourquoi_faux: A concave (diverging) lens has a negative focal length in the real-is-positive convention; it always gives a virtual image.
items.correction_markdown: Use $f = -|f|$ for a concave lens; a negative $v$ means a virtual image.

items.enonce_markdown: A coin lies on the bottom of a thick glass slab of thickness $9.0\ \mathrm{cm}$. The refractive index of the glass is $1.5$. Viewed from directly above, at what apparent depth does the coin appear, and by how much does it seem to be raised?
items.solution_markdown:
$n = \dfrac{\text{real depth}}{\text{apparent depth}}$, so apparent depth $= \dfrac{9.0}{1.5} = 6.0\ \mathrm{cm}$.

Rise $= 9.0 - 6.0 = 3.0\ \mathrm{cm}$.

**The coin appears at 6.0 cm depth, raised by 3.0 cm.**

items.enonce_markdown: A convex lens of focal length $12\ \mathrm{cm}$ forms an image of a candle flame $6.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ high placed $30\ \mathrm{cm}$ from the lens. Using the real-is-positive convention, calculate (a) the image distance, (b) the magnification and (c) the height of the image. State the nature of the image.
items.solution_markdown:
Convention: $u = +30\ \mathrm{cm}$ and $f = +12\ \mathrm{cm}$ (convex lens).

(a) $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{12} - \dfrac{1}{30} = \dfrac{5 - 2}{60} = \dfrac{3}{60} = \dfrac{1}{20}$, so $v = 20\ \mathrm{cm}$. **Image distance = 20 cm.**

(b) $m = \dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{20}{30} = 0.67$. **Magnification = 0.67.**

(c) Image height $= 0.67 \times 6.0 = 4.0\ \mathrm{cm}$. **Height = 4.0 cm.**

$v$ is positive, so the image is **real**, inverted and diminished.

items.enonce_markdown: (a) The refractive index of a type of glass is $1.6$. Calculate its critical angle. (b) A ray travelling inside this glass meets a glass-air boundary at an angle of incidence of $30^\circ$. Does it emerge into the air? If so, find the angle of refraction in the air. (c) A concave lens of focal length $15\ \mathrm{cm}$ forms an image of an object $9.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ high placed $30\ \mathrm{cm}$ from the lens. Find the image distance, nature and height of the image.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\sin c = \dfrac{1}{n} = \dfrac{1}{1.6} = 0.625$, so $c = 38.7^\circ$. **Critical angle = 38.7 degrees.**

(b) $30^\circ < c$, so there is no total internal reflection and the ray emerges. For glass to air: $n = \dfrac{\sin(\text{angle in air})}{\sin(\text{angle in glass})}$, so $\sin r = 1.6 \times \sin 30^\circ = 1.6 \times 0.5 = 0.8$ and $r = 53.1^\circ$. **The ray emerges at 53.1 degrees to the normal.**

(c) Real-is-positive convention: $u = +30\ \mathrm{cm}$ and $f = -15\ \mathrm{cm}$. $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{15} - \dfrac{1}{30} = -\dfrac{3}{30} = -\dfrac{1}{10}$, so $v = -10\ \mathrm{cm}$. The magnification is $\dfrac{10}{30} = \dfrac{1}{3}$ and the height is $\dfrac{9.0}{3} = 3.0\ \mathrm{cm}$.

**The image is virtual, upright and diminished, 10 cm from the lens on the same side as the object, 3.0 cm high.**

items_markdown: Refractive index $n = \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \dfrac{\text{speed in air}}{\text{speed in medium}} = \dfrac{\text{real depth}}{\text{apparent depth}}$ for light entering a medium from air.
Light bends towards the normal entering a denser medium and away from it entering a less dense medium; angles are measured from the normal.
Total internal reflection needs light in the denser medium with $i > c$, where $\sin c = 1/n$.
Lens formula (real-is-positive convention): $\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{u} + \dfrac{1}{v}$ and $m = \dfrac{v}{u}$; state the convention, and remember that a negative $v$ means a virtual image.
A graph of sin i against sin r is a straight line through the origin whose gradient is the refractive index.
